title: Introduction to AWS Secrets Manager
description: Understand why secrets should not live in code and how Secrets Manager secures them.

data.text: Hardcoded connection strings, API keys, and certificates are one of the most common security vulnerabilities in .NET applications. AWS Secrets Manager stores these secrets in a managed, encrypted service.

items: **Secrets** — strings such as database connection strings and API keys
**Keys** — cryptographic keys for encryption and signing
**Certificates** — TLS certificates imported from ACM or uploaded

rows: One secret per environment with IAM policies
Built-in access logs and CloudTrail events
Manual secret updates in every app

data.title: Never commit secrets
data.text: Even in private repos, secrets should not be committed. Use Secrets Manager, environment variables, or AWS App Configuration with IAM roles.

data.title: Create a secret with AWS CLI
data.content:
Create a secret in Secrets Manager for the database connection string.
# Expected output: Secret ARN is returned for use in C# code.
data.code: aws secretsmanager create-secret --name aspnet/connectionstrings/default --description "Default database connection string" --secret-string "Server=tcp:...;Database=BlogDb;User Id=...;Password=...;"

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Secrets Manager replaces hardcoded secrets with centrally managed values
Access is controlled by IAM policies
Secrets can be referenced by Elastic Beanstalk, ECS, and ASP.NET Core
Secrets Manager supports automatic rotation and auditing
data.takeaway: Secrets Manager is the first step in moving secrets out of your code and into a purpose-built AWS service.
